topics.title: Semantic HTML & Page Layout Elements
topics.summary: header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer describe the role of each part of a page.
topics.description:
A **semantic** element tells you what its content *is*, not just how it looks. `<div>` and `<span>` are non-semantic; `<header>`, `<nav>` and `<footer>` are semantic.

### Why semantics?
- **Accessibility** - screen readers can jump between landmarks (nav, main...).
- **SEO** - search engines understand which part is the main content.
- **Maintainability** - `<footer>` is easier to find than the 12th `<div class="x">`.
- **Free default behaviour** - e.g. keyboard and styling support.

### The main layout elements
| Element | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `<header>` | Introductory content / logo / heading of the page or section |
| `<nav>` | Major navigation links |
| `<main>` | The dominant content - **only one visible** per page |
| `<section>` | A thematic group of content, normally with a heading |
| `<article>` | Self-contained content that makes sense alone (blog post, news item, comment) |
| `<aside>` | Related but secondary content (sidebar, ads, tips) |
| `<footer>` | Footer of the page or section (copyright, links) |
| `<figure>`, `<address>`, `<time>` | More semantics |

### section vs article vs div
- Could it be syndicated on its own (RSS)? → `article`.
- A themed chapter with its own heading? → `section`.
- Only a styling wrapper? → `div`.

### Typical page skeleton
```
body
 ├ header (logo + nav)
 ├ main
 │   ├ article
 │   └ aside
 └ footer
```

Landmarks like `header` and `footer` map to ARIA roles *banner* and *contentinfo* only when they are direct children of `<body>`.
keyPoints: Semantic elements describe meaning; div/span do not.
Use one main element per page.
article = standalone content; section = themed group; aside = secondary.
Semantics improve accessibility, SEO and maintainability.
Use div only when no semantic element fits.
pitfalls: Div soup: replacing all semantic tags with divs and classes.
Using section as a generic wrapper with no heading.
Several visible main elements on one page.

topics.title: details & summary (Native Accordion)
topics.summary: Create expandable/collapsible content with zero JavaScript.
topics.description:
`
` creates a **disclosure widget**: content that the user can open and close. `` is the always-visible label (the first child). ```html
What is HTML?

HTML is the standard markup language for web pages.

``` ### Why it is great - Works **without JavaScript**. - Keyboard accessible (Enter/Space toggles) and announced as expanded/collapsed to screen readers. - Perfect for FAQs, "read more", filters and advanced options. ### Attributes - `open` - starts expanded. - `name="group"` - details elements with the same name act as an **exclusive accordion** (opening one closes the others) in modern browsers. ### JavaScript - `details.open` gets/sets the state. - The `toggle` event fires when it opens or closes. ### Styling - The marker is a triangle: style it with `summary::marker`, or hide it with `list-style: none`. - You can animate the content with CSS (e.g. `interpolate-size` / `::details-content` in new browsers) or JavaScript. ### When not to use Do not hide critical information the user must see, and do not use it for tab interfaces (tabs use ARIA roles).
keyPoints: details = widget; summary = visible clickable label.
open attribute makes it start expanded.
Same name attribute makes an exclusive accordion.
Built-in keyboard and screen reader support.
toggle event fires on state change.
pitfalls: Placing something before summary - summary must be the first child.
Hiding essential content inside collapsed details.
Removing the marker and giving no visual cue.

interview.q: What are details and summary used for?
interview.a: To create native expand/collapse content: summary is the visible heading, the rest of details is revealed on click.

interview.q: How do you make several details behave like an accordion?
interview.a: Give them the same name attribute so opening one closes the others.

topics.title: dialog & the popover Attribute
topics.summary: Native modal dialogs with dialog and lightweight popovers with the popover attribute.
topics.description:
Modals and popups used to need big JavaScript libraries. Modern HTML has them built in. ### The dialog element `` is a box that can be shown **modally** or non-modally. ```js dialog.showModal(); // modal: blocks the page, adds a ::backdrop, traps focus, Esc closes dialog.show(); // non-modal dialog.close("ok"); // closes, sets dialog.returnValue ``` Benefits of `showModal()`: focus is moved into the dialog, the rest of the page becomes inert, **Esc closes it**, and the dialog sits in the *top layer* (no z-index battles). ### Closing with a form A form with `method="dialog"` closes the dialog on submit and puts the button's value in `returnValue`: ```html
``` Styling: `dialog::backdrop { background: rgba(0,0,0,.5) }`. ### The popover attribute `popover` turns **any element** into a light-dismiss popup (menus, tooltips, toasts) - no JavaScript: ```html
Hello!
``` - `popover="auto"` (default): closes on click outside or Esc and closes other auto popovers. - `popover="manual"`: you control closing. - `popovertargetaction="show|hide|toggle"`. Use **dialog** for decisions that must block the page and **popover** for non-blocking floating UI.
keyPoints: dialog.showModal() gives a modal with backdrop, focus trapping and Esc.
form method="dialog" closes the dialog and sets returnValue.
popover + popovertarget creates popups without JS.
Both render in the top layer - no z-index issues.
Use dialog for blocking tasks, popover for light UI.
pitfalls: Using the open attribute directly instead of showModal() - no backdrop or focus trap.
Forgetting an accessible name (aria-labelledby) on the dialog.
Using a popover for important confirmations.

topics.title: The head: title, meta, link, base, style, script
topics.summary: Everything that goes inside head and what each element does.
topics.description:
The `<head>` holds metadata - data *about* the page. Order matters a little: put `charset` first.

### Elements allowed in head
| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `<title>` | Page title (tab, bookmarks, search result headline). **Required** |
| `<meta charset="UTF-8">` | Character encoding - within the first 1024 bytes |
| `<meta name="viewport" ...>` | Responsive scaling on mobile |
| `<meta name="description">` | Search snippet |
| `<meta name="theme-color">` | Browser UI colour on mobile |
| `<link rel="stylesheet" href>` | External CSS |
| `<link rel="icon" href>` | Favicon |
| `<link rel="canonical" href>` | Preferred URL for SEO |
| `<link rel="preload / preconnect">` | Resource hints |
| `<base href>` | Base URL for all relative links (use carefully) |
| `<style>` | Internal CSS |
| `<script>` | JavaScript |
| `<noscript>` | Fallback when JS is disabled |

### meta http-equiv
`<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="5;url=/new">` redirects - avoid; use server redirects.

### Favicons and manifests
`<link rel="icon" href="/favicon.ico" sizes="any">`, `<link rel="apple-touch-icon">` and `<link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">` for PWA info.

### A good head template
Charset → viewport → title → description → canonical → icons → CSS → scripts (with `defer`).
keyPoints: title is required; keep it unique per page.
meta charset should be first, ideally in the first 1024 bytes.
link connects CSS, icons, canonical URL and hints.
Use script with defer in the head to avoid blocking.
base changes how ALL relative URLs resolve - use rarely.
pitfalls: Same title on every page.
Placing meta charset after other content.
Using http-equiv refresh for redirects.

examples.title: A well-organised head
examples.code:
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8" />
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
  <title>CodeRevise - Learn HTML Fast</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Revise HTML from basics to advanced with examples." />
  <meta name="theme-color" content="#e34c26" />
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/html" />
  <link rel="icon" href="/favicon.svg" type="image/svg+xml" />
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/main.css" />
  <script src="/js/app.js" defer></script>
</head>

interview.q: Which element in head is mandatory?

interview.a: It tells search engines which URL is the preferred version of a page, avoiding duplicate content.

interview.q: What does the base element do?
interview.a: It sets the base URL against which all relative URLs on the page are resolved.

topics.title: SEO Basics & Meta Tags
topics.summary: Help search engines understand and rank a page: title, description, headings, alt text and robots.
topics.description:
**SEO** (Search Engine Optimization) is making your pages easy for search engines to find, understand and show. HTML does a large part of it.

### The top on-page items
1. **`<title>`** - unique, descriptive, ~50-60 characters, keyword near the start.
2. **`<meta name="description">`** - a ~150-160 character summary shown under the title in results. It does not rank directly but boosts click-through.
3. **One `<h1>`** with a clear heading hierarchy below.
4. **Image `alt` text** and compressed images.
5. **Semantic HTML** and descriptive link text.
6. **Open Graph tags** for social sharing (next topic).

### Meta robots
`<meta name="robots" content="index, follow">` is the default. Use `noindex` to keep a page out of search results and `nofollow` to not follow its links. Per-link control: `rel="nofollow"`.

### meta keywords
`<meta name="keywords">` is **ignored by Google** today. It is harmless but pointless.

### More SEO factors
| Area | Tip |
|---|---|
| Content | Original, useful, matches search intent |
| URLs | Short, readable, hyphen separated |
| Mobile | Responsive layout + viewport meta |
| Speed | Optimised images, defer scripts, fewer requests |
| Links | Internal links to related pages, quality external links |
| Structure | `canonical`, sitemap.xml, robots.txt, structured data |

Good HTML cannot replace good content - it simply removes obstacles.
keyPoints: A unique title and description per page are the basics.
One h1 and a clear heading hierarchy.
alt text, semantic HTML and compressed images help.
robots meta controls indexing; keywords meta is ignored.
Mobile friendliness and speed are ranking factors.
pitfalls: Keyword stuffing in title/description.
Duplicate titles and descriptions across pages.
Accidentally leaving noindex on production pages.

topics.title: Open Graph & Twitter Card Meta Tags
topics.summary: Control how your page looks when shared on WhatsApp, Facebook, LinkedIn and X.
topics.description:
When someone pastes your URL into WhatsApp, Slack, LinkedIn or Facebook, the app fetches the page and reads **Open Graph** meta tags to build a preview card (title, description, image).

### Essential Open Graph tags
```html
<meta property="og:title" content="CodeRevise - Learn HTML Fast">
<meta property="og:description" content="Revise HTML from basics to advanced.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/cover.jpg">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/html">
<meta property="og:type" content="website">
<meta property="og:site_name" content="CodeRevise">
```

Notice they use **`property`**, not `name`.

### Twitter / X cards
```html
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="...">
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/cover.jpg">
```
If Twitter tags are missing, X falls back to Open Graph.

### Image tips
- Use an **absolute URL** (https://...).
- Recommended size ~ 1200x630 px (1.91:1).
- Keep under ~5 MB; JPG/PNG are the safest.
- Add `og:image:alt` for accessibility.

### Testing
Social platforms cache previews. Use their debugger tools (Facebook Sharing Debugger, LinkedIn Post Inspector) to refresh.

### og:type values
`website`, `article`, `video.movie`, `profile`, `product`...
keyPoints: Open Graph uses meta property="og:..." tags.
og:title, og:description, og:image, og:url are the core four.
Use absolute https URLs and ~1200x630 images.
twitter:card selects the X card layout.
Platforms cache previews - use debuggers to refresh.
pitfalls: Using a relative path for og:image.
Using name instead of property for og tags.
Changing the image but not clearing the platform cache.

topics.title: Viewport, Language & Text Direction
topics.summary: Make pages scale properly on phones and declare language and direction for global audiences.
topics.description:
### Responsive viewport meta Mobile browsers pretend to be ~980px wide and shrink the page unless you tell them otherwise: ```html ``` - `width=device-width` - use the real device width. - `initial-scale=1.0` - 100% zoom at load. - Do **not** add `user-scalable=no` or `maximum-scale=1` - it blocks zoom and harms accessibility. Without it, your CSS media queries do not behave as expected on phones. ### Language: lang attribute `` sets the page language. Why it matters: - Screen readers use the correct pronunciation. - Browsers offer the right translation and spell checking, hyphenation. - Search engines serve the right audience. You can override on any element: `

Bonjour

`. Use BCP 47 codes: `en`, `en-US`, `hi`, `ar`, `zh-Hans`. ### Text direction: dir `dir="ltr"` (left-to-right), `dir="rtl"` (Arabic, Hebrew) or `dir="auto"`. `` and `` isolate or override direction for inline text. ### Multi-language sites - `` tells search engines about translated versions. - Always save the file as **UTF-8** and keep `` so Devanagari, Arabic or emoji render correctly. The course sample page is written entirely in Hindi using `lang="hi"`.
keyPoints: viewport meta with width=device-width is required for responsive design.
Never disable user zoom.
lang on html helps screen readers, translation and SEO.
dir="rtl" supports right-to-left languages.
Use UTF-8 for multilingual text.
pitfalls: Missing viewport meta - the page looks tiny on phones.
lang="en" on a Hindi page - screen reader mispronounces text.
Saving the file in a non-UTF-8 encoding.

interview.q: Why do we need the viewport meta tag?
interview.a: Without it mobile browsers render at a wide virtual width and zoom out; width=device-width makes the layout match the device width.

interview.q: Why set lang on the html element?
interview.a: For screen reader pronunciation, translation tools, spell checking and search engine targeting.
